content: Raspberries are the edible fruits of various species within the genus Rubus. The term raspberry originally referred specifically to the European species Rubus idaeus, which remains its standard English name in its native regions. Other species closely related within the subgenus Idaeobatus are also referred to as raspberries. These include: Rubus strigosus (American Raspberry, synonym: Rubus idaeus var. strigosus) Rubus arcticus (Arctic Raspberry) Rubus crataegifolius (Korean Raspberry) Rubus occidentalis (Black Raspberry) Rubus odoratus (Flowering Raspberry) Rubus phoenicolasius (Wine Raspberry) Rubus leucodermis (Whitebark or Western Raspberry, also known as Blue Raspberry in its native regions) Raspberries are a significant commercial fruit crop cultivated extensively in temperate regions worldwide. Many modern commercial raspberry cultivars are hybrids derived from Rubus idaeus and Rubus strigosus. Cultivation Raspberries are grown for both the fresh fruit market and for commercial processing into products such as individually quick frozen (IQF) fruit, purée, juice, or dried fruit used in various grocery items. Traditionally, raspberries were a mid-summer crop, but advancements in technology, cultivars, and transportation now allow for year-round availability. Optimal growth requires ample sunlight and water, though excessive moisture or poorly drained soils can lead to Phytophthora root rot, a serious pest issue for red raspberries. Raspberries thrive in moist temperate regions and are relatively easy to grow. However, they tend to spread aggressively if not pruned. Escaped raspberry plants often appear as garden weeds, propagated by seeds dispersed through bird droppings. Two main types of raspberries are commercially available: 1. Summer-bearing varieties: These produce abundant fruit on second-year canes (floricanes) during a short period in mid-summer. 2. Ever-bearing or double-bearing varieties: These produce fruit on first-year canes (primocanes) in late summer and fall, in addition to the summer crop on second-year canes. Raspberries can be cultivated in USDA hardiness zones 3 to 9. They are traditionally planted in winter as dormant canes, though the use of tender plug plants from tissue culture has become increasingly common. A specialized production method called long cane production involves growing canes for one year in northern climates (e.g., Scotland or Washington State) to meet chilling requirements for proper bud break. These canes are then transplanted to warmer climates (e.g., Spain) to produce an early-season crop. Plants should be spaced approximately 1 meter apart in fertile, well-drained soil. Raised beds or ridges are often used to prevent root rot. Raspberry flowers are a significant nectar source for honeybees. The plants are vigorous and can become invasive, spreading through basal shoots (suckers) and underground shoots that develop roots and new plants. This ability to propagate can lead to raspberries overtaking gardens if not managed. The fruit is harvested when it turns deep red and detaches easily from the torus/receptacle. This is when the fruit is at its ripest and sweetest. Excess fruit can be preserved as raspberry jam or frozen. Raspberry leaves, which have an astringent flavor, can be used fresh or dried in herbal and medicinal teas. In herbal medicine, they are reputed to help regulate menstruation. Each raspberry weighs approximately 4 grams and consists of around 100 drupelets, each containing a juicy pulp and a single tiny seed. Raspberry bushes can yield several pounds of fruit annually. Unlike blackberries, raspberries have a hollow core once removed from the receptacle. Cultivars Numerous raspberry cultivars have been developed, including thornless and more upright varieties that do not require staking. Crossbreeding with black raspberries (Rubus occidentalis) has produced purple raspberries, while hybridization with other Rubus species has resulted in fruits like boysenberries and loganberries. Cultivars with yellow fruit are sometimes referred to as golden raspberries. Nutrients and Potential Health Benefits Raspberries are rich in polyphenol antioxidants, including anthocyanin pigments, which are associated with potential protective effects against various human diseases. Their aggregate fruit structure contributes to their high dietary fiber content, making them one of the plant foods with the highest fiber levels, up to 20% of their total weight. Raspberries are an excellent source of vitamin C (30 mg per cup, about 50% of the daily value), manganese (about 60% of the daily value), and dietary fiber (30% of the daily value). They also contain significant amounts of B vitamins (B1, B2, B3), folic acid, magnesium, copper, and iron. Raspberries rank highly among fruits for antioxidant strength, primarily due to their dense content of ellagic acid (from ellagitannins), quercetin, gallic acid, anthocyanins, cyanidins, pelargonidins, catechins, kaempferol, and salicylic acid. These polyphenolic antioxidants are under active research for their promising health benefits. Due to their high levels of antioxidant vitamin C and polyphenols, raspberries have an ORAC (Oxygen Radical Absorbance Capacity) value of approximately 4900 per 100 grams, placing them among the top-ranked ORAC fruits. For comparison, cranberries and wild blueberries have around 9000 ORAC units, while apples average 2800. Preliminary medical research suggests that regular consumption of raspberries may offer benefits against: Inflammation Pain Cancer Cardiovascular disease Diabetes Allergies Age-related cognitive decline Degeneration of eyesight with aging Diseases and Pests Raspberries are sometimes targeted by the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species (butterflies and moths). For more information, refer to the list of Lepidoptera that feed on Rubus.
